hints: Notice this question asks about two completely different forces, the strong bond inside each molecule and the weak force between molecules.
Think about atomic size going from chlorine to iodine, the atoms get bigger so the bond gets longer and orbital overlap gets poorer.
Now think the opposite way for forces between molecules, more electrons means a bigger, more polarisable cloud and stronger temporary dipoles.
walkthrough:
**Separate inside from between**

Think of each halogen as $\text{Cl}_2$, $\text{Br}_2$, $\text{I}_2$. There are two ideas here. Covalent bond strength is the force inside one molecule, between the two atoms. Van der Waals forces are the weak attractions between separate molecules.

Rule to remember:
$$\text{intramolecular (covalent) } \neq \text{ intermolecular (van der Waals)}$$

**Covalent bonds get weaker down the group**

Going down Group 17, atoms get larger. The outer orbitals are bigger and more diffuse.

This means longer bonds and poorer overlap, so the shared pair is held less strongly. Bond energy decreases from $\text{Cl}_2$ to $\text{Br}_2$ to $\text{I}_2$.

**Van der Waals forces get stronger down the group**

Van der Waals forces here are London dispersion forces. They depend on number of electrons and how easily the electron cloud can be distorted.

Going down, molecules have many more electrons ($\text{Cl}_2$ has 34, $\text{I}_2$ has 106). Larger clouds are more polarisable, so temporary dipoles are stronger. That is why chlorine is a gas, bromine is a liquid and iodine is a solid at room temperature.

**Put the two trends together**

Covalent strength decreases, but van der Waals strength increases. That combination matches only one row in the table.

options.A: Half right and half wrong. Covalent bonds do decrease, but van der Waals forces do not decrease. More electrons down the group gives stronger London forces, shown by rising melting and boiling points.
options.B: Correct. Longer, weaker covalent bonds mean bond strength decreases from $\text{Cl}_2$ to $\text{I}_2$. More electrons and greater polarisability mean van der Waals forces between molecules increase.
options.C: Both trends reversed. Students choose this if they confuse inside and between. Larger atoms give poorer overlap so covalent bonds get weaker, not stronger, and larger electron clouds give stronger, not weaker, dispersion forces.
options.D: Half right and half wrong. Van der Waals forces do increase, but covalent bonds do not increase. Increasing atomic radius and bond length weakens the covalent bond down the group.
